title: Emma Smith is called as an elect lady with her own work
setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation for his wife, Emma Hale Smith, at Harmony, Pennsylvania, in July 1830. Emma had been baptized at Colesville, New York, on 28 June, but opposition delayed her confirmation. The earliest manuscript gives only the year, and the July date first appears in the 1833 Book of Commandments. It was the first known revelation of Joseph’s addressed to a woman. In 1835 Emma and William W. Phelps compiled the church’s first hymnal.
summary: The revelation speaks to Emma Smith as a daughter in the Lord’s kingdom. It promises to preserve her life and give her an inheritance in Zion if she is faithful. It forgives her sins and calls her “an elect lady”. It tells her not to murmur over things she has not been shown. Her calling is to comfort Joseph, serve as his scribe, and be ordained to expound scripture and exhort the church. She is to lay aside the things of this world and make a selection of sacred hymns. The text warns against pride and promises a crown of righteousness if she keeps the commandments. It closes by saying this is the Lord’s voice to all.

contextNote.title: Why a hymnbook belongs in a revelation
contextNote.text: Verse 11 gives Emma an unusual task: to select sacred hymns for the church. Verse 12 gives the reason for it. The Lord’s soul “delighteth in the song of the heart”. The verse then treats such singing as a kind of prayer. Because it is prayer, it can be answered “with a blessing upon their heads”. Verse 13 carries the thought forward by telling Emma to “lift up thy heart and rejoice”. In this passage a hymn is worship that God hears and answers, not only music for a meeting.

ldsText: The Come, Follow Me 2025 lesson “Seek for the Things of a Better World” takes its title from verse 10 of this revelation to Emma. Verse 12 calls “the song of the righteous” a prayer; which hymn has felt like a prayer to you, and what blessing followed?
reviewNote: Read all 16 verses. Official heading gives Harmony, July 1830, to Emma Smith, and refers to the heading of section 24. JSP historical introduction read for the date (earliest copy gives only 1830; July first appears in the 1833 Book of Commandments), Emma’s 28 June baptism, the ordering question among the three July revelations, and the 1835 hymnal with W. W. Phelps. Fact-check 2026-10-12: setting said “first” revelation to a woman; JSP says only that no earlier women recipients are known, so changed to “first known”.
